fields.title: Gryada: Two Quarters Without Visible Results
fields.summary: The lead engineer asks to rewrite the engine. The commercial director says we won't survive this.
fields.decisionPrompt: What will you propose to the committee?
fields.brief/role: You are the product manager of the platform team.
fields.brief/company: Gryada is a fictional company of 400 people that sells a supply chain planning system.
fields.brief/context: The lead engineer proposed replacing the planning engine—the component that calculates plans—in two quarters with four people. The current engine was written eight years ago by people who have since left, and it now blocks three roadmap items critical for the commercial team. The commercial director publicly stated that 'we won't survive' two quarters without visible results in a year when the company is falling behind its growth target.
fields.brief/objective: Make a decision that can be defended with both money and timelines.
fields.brief/constraints: There are four people on the platform team. Two quarters is half a year. The growth target is not being met. No new hires this year.
fields.brief/task: Choose a solution and justify it.
fields.learnTakeaway/title: A long technical project is defended with a metric, not a promise
fields.learnTakeaway/body: A committee that remembers a failed rewrite won't believe a deadline—and they will be right. What works is a visible weekly progress metric and a pre-defined point where the work can be stopped. And the choice between a rewrite, hardware, and postponement is calculated in money: the blocked pipeline on one side, the cost of delay for a year on the other.
fields.evidenceCards/0/content:
«The engine recalculates the entire plan on every change. With ten thousand items, this was fine; our largest clients now have 400 thousand, and recalculation takes 6–11 minutes. Everything downstream inherits this latency.

The rewrite introduces incremental recalculation: we only compute what changed. Expected time for a typical edit is under 4 seconds.

Two quarters, four people. First quarter—new engine runs alongside the old one, verifying results on real data; second quarter—migrating clients.

Verification provides a visible weekly progress metric: the percentage of plans where both engines match».
fields.evidenceCards/2/content:
1. Hardware: moving the largest clients to larger machines reduced recalculation by about 30% last year and cost an extra 3.6 million ₽ per month. Another 30% is available for about 8 million ₽ per month, and the head of infrastructure says that's the end of the road.

2. Caching in front of the current engine: two people for six weeks. Speeds up repeat views of unchanged plans, but doesn't help with edits—which is what the complaints are about.

3. Narrow rewrite of only the recalculation path, without changing the data model: one quarter, four people. Expected speedup is about 3x (down to 2–4 minutes), which unlocks scenario comparison but not collaborative work.

4. Do nothing: recalculation time grows with client size, at about 15% per year.
fields.evidenceCards/3/content:
Gryada tried to rewrite the platform three years ago. Estimated at six months, it dragged on for fourteen, and was abandoned with only partially merged work. The current engine still contains two half-migrated modules.

Several people from that project sit on the committee that approves the plan.

The lead engineer joined after that and has since delivered two major projects on time, both with intermediate checkpoints.

Cash runway: the company is profitable, but the growth target is not being met, and the board is watching.

Head of engineering: «If the committee has nothing to look at every two weeks, they will stop it by week five».
fields.decisionOptions/0/label: Full rewrite with verification matching and a checkpoint
fields.decisionOptions/0/description: Take two quarters, make the percentage of matching plans during parallel engine runs the visible progress metric, and pre-schedule a week when the committee can stop or continue the work.
fields.decisionOptions/0/consequence:
The main objection here is not technical, but historical: three years ago, six months turned into fourteen, and people from that project sit on the committee. The answer to this is not a promise, but an observable metric: the percentage of plans where the new engine matches the old one grows every week and is visible to everyone.
A checkpoint in week eight with a pre-defined condition for continuation shifts the conversation from 'do we believe you' to 'let's look at the number.'
To the commercial director, you bring not 'two quarters of silence,' but a list: 330 million ₽ of pipeline is blocked by three items, and all three depend on recalculation; one major client made this a condition for renewal in two quarters.
You rule out hardware as an alternative with numbers: 8 million ₽ per month for 30% is 96 million ₽ per year for a delay, and that's the end of the road.
By the end of the first quarter, verification shows 98% matches, and the committee allows the project to continue.
Compromise: half a year without new features, and the growth target for this year will not be met—you state this directly rather than hiding it.
fields.decisionOptions/1/label: Narrow rewrite of the recalculation path in one quarter
fields.decisionOptions/1/description: Take a 3x speedup in one quarter, unlock what it unlocks, and decide on the data model later.
fields.decisionOptions/1/consequence:
One quarter instead of two, which is significantly easier to get through the committee given their memory of the past failure.
Recalculation drops from 6–11 minutes to 2–4. Scenario comparison is unlocked—that's 210 million ₽ out of 330 million ₽ in the pipeline.
Collaborative planning remains blocked: it is limited by locking during recalculation, not by its duration.
A year later, recalculation time grows again by 15% along with client size, and the conversation about a full rewrite returns—only now with a quarter already spent and some team members gone.
Compromise: you got two-thirds of the benefit in half the time while leaving the root cause untouched; for a year with an unmet growth target, this is a sensible trade-off.
fields.decisionOptions/2/label: Two on the rewrite, two on the roadmap
fields.decisionOptions/2/description: Maintain a visible stream of features and run the rewrite in the background over four quarters.
fields.decisionOptions/2/consequence:
On paper, this looks like a compromise, and the committee is most willing to accept it.
Four quarters instead of two means the rewrite will overlap with changing priorities, vacations, and two release cycles; this is exactly how the previous project died.
Two developers on the current engine achieve little: the three blocked items require recalculation changes, which won't happen until the work is finished.
By the fourth quarter, half of the rewrite is merged, half is not—the exact state from which the current engine already contains two half-migrated modules.
Compromise: trying to avoid a choice doubles the timeline and repeats the very failure mode this company is known for.
fields.decisionOptions/3/label: Buy time with hardware and postpone to next year
fields.decisionOptions/3/description: Spend an extra 8 million ₽ per month on infrastructure for the largest clients, release what is possible on the old engine, and return to the issue once the growth target is met.
fields.decisionOptions/3/consequence:
The decision is made quickly and relieves pressure in the quarter: recalculation drops by another 30%, to 4–7 minutes.
96 million ₽ per year is spent on a delay, while the head of infrastructure explicitly states that there is no road beyond this.
The three blocked items remain blocked: scenario comparison doubles the recalculation cost, turning 4 minutes into 8.
A year later, recalculation grows by 15%, eating up the purchased speedup, and the client who made it a condition for renewal has already made their decision.
Compromise: time was bought at a price comparable to the team's salary, and it was wasted on nothing.
fields.rubric/remediation/0/gap: Economics are calculated for the company as a whole, rather than per client and by segment
fields.rubric/remediation/1/gap: The decision was made without a buffer, burn rate, and horizon
